title: Cut one link: what do the others carry?
hook: Two friend groups, two links between them. Cut one and watch the shortest paths move.

knows: a person between two groups carries many shortest paths (broker-between-two-groups)
doesNotKnow: that link loads must be recounted after every cut
that cutting the busiest link and recounting splits a network into its communities (Girvan–Newman)

misconception: Rank the links by how many shortest paths they carry once, then cut down the list; removing one link leaves the others' loads where they were.
objective: The learner can explain that cutting one of the two links between two groups sends all 24 cross-group shortest paths through the other (12 to 24) and shifts loads inside the groups, so link counts must be recounted after every cut, which is the Girvan–Newman method: cut the busiest link, recount, repeat until the network splits into its groups.

claims.text: At the start each of the two links between the groups (5–6 and 3–7) carries 12 shortest paths, and no other link carries more than 5.
claims.source: Builder's node Brandes-style count 2026-10-14 on the 17-link edge list in Demo.tsx (every unordered pair once; a pair with k shortest paths gives 1/k to each): 5-6 = 12, 3-7 = 12, others 0-1 4, 0-2 4, 0-3 5, 0-4 2, 0-5 5, 2-3 5, 3-4 4, 4-5 4, 1-5 5, 6-7 4, 7-8 4, 8-9 1, 6-9 4, 6-8 4, 7-9 4. Demo.tsx loads() computes the labels the stage draws. Fact-checker: re-run with an independent method (enumerate shortest paths per pair). | FC pass 35 (fact-checker, 2026-10-14): VERIFIED. Own port of loads() plus an independent brute force that lists every shortest path per pair and gives each 1/k: both give 5–6 = 12, 3–7 = 12; the largest other link is 5 (0–3, 0–5, 2–3, 1–5). The two methods agree on 3,543 sampled cut sets (0 mismatches).

claims.text: After one between-group link is cut, the other carries 24: all 6 × 4 = 24 pairs with one person in each group must use it, so its count doubles; links inside the groups change too (cutting 5–6: 0–3 goes 5 → 12.5; cutting 3–7: 0–5 goes 5 → 12.5).
claims.source: Every cross pair's shortest paths all cross the one remaining bridge. Builder's node 2026-10-14: cut 3-7 gives 5-6 = 24, 0-5 = 12.5, 4-5 = 8; cut 5-6 gives 3-7 = 24, 0-3 = 12.5, 3-4 = 8. The stage trace quotes the inner link whose count changed most. | FC pass 35 (fact-checker, 2026-10-14): VERIFIED. Own port: cut 5–6 gives 3–7 = 24 and 0–3 5 → 12.5 (the largest inner change, so the trace names it); cut 3–7 gives 5–6 = 24 and 0–5 5 → 12.5. Enumerated all 10,608 connected inner-cut states the learner can reach before the first bridge cut: the remaining bridge always carries exactly 24 after it, and 5 to 19 before it, never more. So the reveal's 'doubled to 24' / 'rose to 24' branch is never false.

claims.text: After both between-group links are cut, the network is two groups of 6 and 4.
claims.source: The only links between {0..5} and {6..9} are 5-6 and 3-7; each group is connected inside. Demo.tsx pieces(). | FC pass 35 (fact-checker, 2026-10-14): VERIFIED. pieces(): with 5–6 and 3–7 both cut and nothing else, there are 2 components, {0..5} and {6..9}, so isGroups is true, sizes 6 and 4. Any other disconnection freezes the stage with 'A piece broke off, not the two groups', so the 'two groups of 6 and 4' text only shows on that state.

claims.text: The Girvan–Newman method cuts the busiest link, recounts every link, and repeats.
claims.source: v2 2026-10-16 (r14 finding 3, fallback): the told sentence 'A list ranked once goes stale after every cut' is cut from the reveal (in this network the once-ranked list cuts the same two bridges as the recount, so it could not be shown; departure for cm-cs); reveal now 'The Girvan–Newman method cuts the busiest link, recounts every link, and repeats.' Reset to unverified because the learner-visible text changed. | v1 record: Girvan and Newman (2002), 'Community structure in social and biological networks', PNAS 99(12): 7821-7826 (remove the edge of highest betweenness, recalculate betweenness for all affected edges, repeat); Easley and Kleinberg (2010), Networks, Crowds, and Markets, ch. 3, section 3.6. Not opened by the builder; fact-checker confirms attribution. | FC pass 35 (fact-checker, 2026-10-14): HELD UNVERIFIED. The reveal sentence matches the claim. Attributing the cut, recount, repeat procedure to Girvan–Newman rests on Girvan and Newman 2002 (PNAS) and Easley and Kleinberg ch. 3. Neither could be opened (DNS failure, proxy 403). 'Goes stale after every cut' is shown on stage (c2), but the attribution needs the source. Left unverified. | FC pass 38 (fact-checker, 2026-10-14): VERIFIED on an opened source: NetworkX girvan_newman() (raw GitHub networkx/networkx, networkx/algorithms/community/centrality.py, opened 2026-10-14). Its docstring says the Girvan–Newman method 'removes the ... edge with the highest betweenness centrality, at each step', and its default most_valuable_edge() calls edge_betweenness_centrality(G) again on the cut graph each time. So the method recounts after every cut. Demo.tsx defines a link's number as its edge betweenness (Brandes), so 'busiest link' means highest betweenness. Girvan and Newman 2002 (PNAS) and E&K 3.6 were not opened.

claims.text: The number on a link is the shortest paths it carries: each pair of people counted once, a pair with several shortest paths sharing its 1 evenly among them. Stage: 'Number on a link: shortest paths it carries.' before any cut; while any count is fractional, 'Each pair counts 1, split evenly over its tied shortest paths.'
claims.source: v2 2026-10-16 (r14 finding 2): the sharing clause is now on the stage message whenever a count on the stage is fractional (Demo.tsx fractional()); reset to unverified because the learner-visible text changed. Convention unchanged: loads() is Brandes edge betweenness, unordered pairs, 1/k split. | v1 record: Edge betweenness as defined by Girvan and Newman (2002) and computed by Brandes (2001), 'A faster algorithm for betweenness centrality', J. Math. Sociology 25(2); unordered pairs, split evenly over shortest paths. Stage legend: 'Number on a link: shortest paths it carries.' | FC pass 35 (fact-checker, 2026-10-14): VERIFIED. Convention matches the code: loads() loops a < t (each unordered pair once) and adds sg[a][u]·sg[t][v]/sg[a][t] per edge, i.e. the pair's 1 split evenly over its shortest paths. My independent path enumeration gives identical labels. Stage legend: 'Number on a link: shortest paths it carries.' The Brandes and Girvan–Newman names are in the source field only, not on stage.

recall.question: You rank a network's links by shortest paths carried, then cut the top one. Before cutting the next, what should you do?
options: Cut the second link on the old list
Cut the link with the fewest paths
recall.why: A cut reroutes shortest paths, so counts change (a remaining bridge can double). Girvan–Newman recounts after every cut, then cuts the new busiest link.
